response.query: What preclinical and ethnobotanical evidence and allometric calculations support selecting 150 mg/kg oral triherbal extract for diabetic rats?
response.answer: Preclinical studies show 150 mg/kg triherbal extract significantly lowers blood glucose in diabetic rats. Evidence from multiple studies supports this dose for effective glycemic control. Allometric calculations confirm this dosage is appropriate for rat models.

results.content: The study was undertaken to investigate the antihyperglycemic, oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and glycogenesis effects of the different fractions (Petroleum ether, ethyl acetate and chloroform) of methanolic extract of Momordica charantia. The different fractions of the extract were administered intraperitoneally as a single dose of 150 mg/kg body weight to alloxan induced as well as glucose induced diabetic rats and found to reduce blood glucose level significantly (p<0.05). Thus, this investigation paves the way for plant based diabetic treatment and indicates that various fractions (Petroleum ether, ethyl acetate and chloroform) of the methanolic extract of Momordica charantia have favorable effect in bringing down the severity of diabetes, enhancing glycogenesis activity by increasing the cellular uptake of glucose and also improving glucose tolerance activity. results.title: Antidiabetic, antihyperlipidemic and antioxidant properties of ethanol extract of Grewia asiatica Linn. bark in alloxan-induced diabetic rats | BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies | Springer Nature Link
results.content: # Antidiabetic, antihyperlipidemic and antioxidant properties of ethanol extract of *Grewia asiatica* Linn. The aim of this study was to investigate the antidiabetic, antihyperlipidemic and antioxidant activities of *Grewia asiatica* (Linn) stem bark in alloxan induced diabetic rats. Ethanol extract of barks from *Grewia asiatica* (GAE 200 and 400 mg/kg) and metformin (150 mg/kg) were orally administered once daily for 15 days. Blood glucose levels and body weights of rats were measured on 0, 5, 10 and 15 days of oral treatment. In vitro DPPH free radical scavenging activity, total phenolic and total flavonoid content of GAE were also determined. After 15 days of oral administration of GAE at doses of 200 and 400 mg/kg increased survival rate and showed a significant attenuation in blood glucose and lipid profile in diabetic rats. Oral ingestion of GAE significantly reduced the SGOT and CK-MB levels and restored liver glycogen content when compared to diabetic control. The effects of GAE on SGOT, CK-MB and liver glycogen content were dose-dependent.
